Slides (black — the pancreatic-masses part of Dr. Aloraini's combined deck), the doctor's notes (green), every gift (red) and the Aldughaither summary (grey, at the end).

Anatomy & overview

  • The coeliac axis gives the common hepatic, splenic and left gastric arteries; the pancreas is also supplied by the GDA and SMA branches — their involvement decides resectability in adenocarcinoma.
LesionTypeKey point (doctor)
AdenocarcinomaSolid, malignant~90% of solid pancreatic lesions — malignant until proven otherwise
PseudocystBenign cysticComplication of pancreatitis; treated only if symptomatic
PNETSolid, low-grade malignantUncommon, variable hormones, hypervascular
Any pancreatic mass is malignant until proven otherwise → urgent surgical/oncology referral.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (PNET)

  • Rare, low-grade malignant; 60% non-functional (and these are more malignant); can occur in the duodenum, peripancreatic tissue, stomach, colon; most found incidentally.
  • Non-functional: asymptomatic, found incidentally; symptoms from mass effect (pain ± jaundice). Diagnosis: serum chromogranin A, 24-h urine 5-HIAA.
  • Non-functional management: no special pre-op preparation · > 2 cm or malignant features → resection · 1–2 cm → observe or resect by site/patient · < 1 cm → observe, or enucleation if removed. 5-year survival ~30–50%.
  • 1–2 cm is individualised: elderly/high-risk → observe; young/healthy → favour resection (lifetime risk, loss to follow-up). A large tumour with few symptoms is concerning — diagnosis is often delayed.
  • MEN 1 (AD): 80% hyperparathyroidism, 80–100% PNET, 50% gastrinomas, most multiple. VHL: 10–17% PNET, 98% non-functional.
  • Localisation: CT/MRI (hypervascular; non-functional larger, insulinomas/gastrinomas smaller) · octreotide (SRS) scan (well-differentiated G1/G2) · FDG-PET (high-grade G3) · EUS + FNA (more sensitive than CT/MRI for < 3 cm; Ki-67) · angiography, portal venous sampling, arterial stimulation · surgical exploration as last resort.

Functional PNETs

TumourSyndromeDiagnosisTreatment
InsulinomaMost common functional, mostly benign; Whipple's triad: fasting hypoglycaemic symptoms, glucose 40–50 mg/dL, relief with glucoseC-peptide + insulin/glucose ratio > 0.3Local resection / enucleation
GastrinomaZollinger–Ellison: hypergastrinaemia, severe/recurrent peptic ulcers, diarrhoea; most in the duodenum (gastrinoma triangle)Fasting gastrin > 1000 pg/mL, EGDPPI for hypersecretion; resection (high metastatic risk)
VIPomaVerner–Morrison: profuse watery diarrhoea 3–5 L/day persisting with fasting → hypokalaemia, acidosisVIP > 1000 pg/mLResection
GlucagonomaLarge (5–10 cm); 4 Ds: diabetes, dermatitis (necrolytic migratory erythema), DVT, depressionFasting glucagon > 1000 (normal ≤ 50)Improve nutrition → aggressive resection
SomatostatinomaVery rare; steatorrhoea, diabetes, hypochlorhydria, gallstonesFasting somatostatin > 100Nutrition → aggressive resection
  • Insulinoma = most benign/best survival; somatostatinoma among the most aggressive. Necrolytic migratory erythema → glucagonoma.
  • Principles: surgery is the mainstay; octreotide controls symptoms; debulking of liver metastases has a role; systemic therapy for unresectable/progressing disease; high recurrence → close follow-up.
  • Unlike adenocarcinoma, metastatic PNET may still benefit from debulking (liver = first metastatic site).
  • Recurrent ulcers resistant to PPI, markedly high fasting gastrin, diarrhoea → Zollinger–Ellison syndrome 442 ×2; commonest site of gastrinoma outside the pancreas → duodenum. 441
  • Hypoglycaemia relieved by juice + pancreatic tail mass → confirm insulinoma with high C-peptide (insulin/glucose ratio > 0.3). 436 ×2

Serous cystadenoma (honeycomb, central scar) · mucinous cystic neoplasm

  • Why amylase differs: MCN doesn't communicate with the duct → low amylase; IPMN communicates → high amylase.
  • Main-duct IPMN: MD dilatation, columnar metaplasia, malignant 60–80%; pain, weight loss, pancreatitis, jaundice; MD > 10 mm = high risk → resection.
  • Side-branch IPMN: malignancy correlates with size; worrisome: mural nodule/wall thickening, enhancing solid component, growth; symptoms (jaundice, pain, diabetes).

Main-duct IPMN · branch-duct IPMN (CT)

Asymptomatic side-branch IPMNFollow-up
< 1 cmCT/MRI yearly
1–3 cmRepeat imaging every 6 months for 2 years, then yearly
Resect ifSymptomatic with worrisome features · > 3 cm · main-duct or mixed type
  • Numbers: main duct 10 mm = high risk; side branch 3 cm = surgical threshold. Non-invasive IPMN after resection → no chemo. Invasive cancer 5-year survival ~50–60%.
  • Asymptomatic 70-year-old, incidental 2.5-cm side-branch IPMN, main duct normal → CT every 6 months. 437
  • Incidental IPMN with main-duct dilatation 12 mm → surgical resection (distal pancreatectomy). 436

Pancreatic adenocarcinoma

  • Most common pancreatic mass (~90%). Risk factors: smoking, diabetes, obesity, chronic pancreatitis, age > 50; hereditary — BRCA2, cystic fibrosis, Lynch, Peutz–Jeghers (highest), FAP.
  • Late presentation; by location: jaundice, weight loss, abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting.
  • Investigations: CA 19-9 (most sensitive and specific marker — falsely high with hyperbilirubinaemia) · triphasic CT and/or MRI/MRCP (hypoattenuation, PD dilatation, CBD dilatation, double-duct sign) · PET · ERCP + brushing · EUS ± FNA.
  • Relieve the biliary obstruction first, then reassess CA 19-9. PNET hypervascular vs adenocarcinoma hypovascular.
Double-duct sign (dilated pancreatic duct + CBD) → pancreatic head malignancy.
  • 67-year-old, painless progressive jaundice, palpable gallbladder → carcinoma of the head of the pancreas 438 ×9; Courvoisier's law → palpable gallbladder: jaundice unlikely to be due to a stone. 429 ×2
  • Tumour marker for pancreatic head tumour → CA 19-9. 436
  • Management: tissue diagnosis is NOT needed for upfront surgery (ERCP brushing yield ~20–30%; don't delay curative surgery) · no surgery in metastatic disease · head → Whipple · body/tail → distal pancreatectomy + splenectomy.

Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) · distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy

  • Whipple removes: pancreatic head, uncinate process, duodenum, distal CBD; reconstruction: pancreaticojejunostomy, hepaticojejunostomy, gastrojejunostomy.
  • Adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head → pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple). 436
  • Resectability (head): resectable / borderline / unresectable. Borderline = severe SMV–portal impingement; short-segment reconstructible SMV occlusion; < 180° SMA abutment; reconstructible hepatic-artery abutment. High morbidity and mortality operation.
  • Resectability depends on whether involved vessels can be safely reconstructed.
  • Body/tail: late presentation, worse prognosis; less morbid surgery than Whipple.
  • Chemo: all patients need chemotherapy (adjuvant or neoadjuvant): gemcitabine or 5-FU/leucovorin or FOLFIRINOX; unresectable/borderline → chemoradiation; operate 6–8 weeks after neoadjuvant.
  • Obstruction & metastases: 40–50% metastatic at presentation; exocrine/endocrine insufficiency; CBD obstruction → stent or hepaticojejunostomy; gastric outlet obstruction → gastrojejunostomy; palliative chemo/RT. 5-year survival with resection + chemo ~15–35%.
  • Unexpected metastases at surgery → abort the resection. Prefer endoscopic stents over surgical bypass (faster to chemo).

Other pancreatic lesions

  • Solid pseudopapillary tumour: young women (22–38), solid + cystic, mostly benign → surgery even with metastases.
  • Metastases to the pancreas: 60% from RCC, ~50% asymptomatic, hypervascular lesions are more likely metastases; RCC metastases benefit from surgery.
  • Hypervascular pancreatic tail lesion years after RCC resection → distal pancreatectomy. 437

Clinical Presentation
A. Symptoms
Head of Pancreas Tumors (More Common, Earlier Diagnosis)
  • Painless jaundice (biliary obstruction).
  • Weight loss & anorexia (~80%).
  • Pruritus (due to bile salt accumulation).
  • Dark urine & pale stools (obstructive jaundice).
  • Epigastric pain → Radiates to the back (~25%).
  • Palpable, nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign).
Body/Tail Tumors (More Advanced, Later Diagnosis)
  • Abdominal pain (often severe, radiates to back).
  • Weight loss & cachexia (~80%).
  • Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau’s sign, ~10%).
  • New-onset diabetes (~25%).
B. Signs
  • Jaundice & pruritus (bile duct compression).
  • Palpable epigastric mass (~10%).
  • Hepatomegaly & ascites (liver metastases).
  • Virchow’s node (left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy).
  • Sister Mary Joseph’s nodule (periumbilical metastasis).
  • Blumer’s shelf (rectal shelf mass, peritoneal metastasis).
Diagnosis
A. Laboratory Tests
  • ↑ CA 19-9 (>1000 U/mL highly specific but NOT diagnostic).
  • ↑ Bilirubin & ALP (biliary obstruction).
  • Mild ↑ AST/ALT (liver involvement).
  • ↑ CEA (~60% of cases, nonspecific).
  • Glucose intolerance/new-onset diabetes (~25%).
B. Imaging Studies
CT scan (Initial Test)
  • Multiphase contrast-enhanced pancreatic protocol CT is first-line.
  • Shows pancreatic mass, ductal dilation, vascular invasion, metastases.
MRI/MRCP
  • Alternative for better soft tissue contrast & duct evaluation.
  • Helpful if uncertain diagnosis or allergic to contrast.
EUS + FNA (Endoscopic Ultrasound + Biopsy)
  • Most sensitive test for small tumors (<2 cm).
  • Allows guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) for histologic confirmation.
ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography)
  • Used only if biliary obstruction is unclear.
  • Shows "double duct sign" (dilated pancreatic + common bile duct).
PET-CT
  • Detects occult metastases.
  • Used in staging or suspected metastatic disease.
Laparoscopy
  • Done before surgery to assess for peritoneal spread.
Staging & Resectability
TNM Staging System
  • T1-T2: Confined to pancreas.
  • T3-T4: Invades major vessels or nearby structures.
  • N1-N2: Lymph node involvement.
  • M1: Distant metastases (liver, lung, peritoneum).
Resectability Criteria
  • Resectable: No major vessel invasion or distant metastases.
  • Borderline Resectable: Involves SMV, PV, or hepatic artery (partial contact).
  • Unresectable: Encases SMA, CA, IVC, distant metastases.
Treatment Options
1. Surgical Resection (Only 15-20% of cases)
  • Curative option for localized disease.
  • Whipple Procedure (Pancreaticoduodenectomy)
  • For tumors in the pancreatic head.
  • Removes head of pancreas, duodenum, gallbladder, CBD, part of stomach/jejunum.
  • Distal Pancreatectomy + Splenectomy
  • For tumors in the body/tail.
  • Total Pancreatectomy (rare, for diffuse disease).
  • Complications: Pancreatic fistula delayed gastric emptying, anastomotic leaks.
2. Neoadjuvant Therapy (For Borderline Resectable Tumors)
  • Chemotherapy ± radiation before surgery to shrink the tumor.
  • Regimens:
  • FOLFIRINOX (most effective but toxic).
  • Gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel (less toxic, well-tolerated).
3. Adjuvant Chemotherapy (Post-Surgery)
  • Gemcitabine ± Capecitabine (Improves survival).
  • FOLFIRINOX (For fit patients, best survival benefit).
4. Palliative Therapy (For Metastatic/Unresectable Tumors)
  • Chemotherapy (FOLFIRINOX or Gemcitabine-based regimens).
  • Endoscopic biliary stenting (for obstructive jaundice).
  • Celiac plexus block (for severe pain).
  • Palliative surgery (gastrojejunostomy for gastric outlet obstruction).
  • Radiation therapy (pain control in metastases).
Prognosis
Overall:
  • 5-year survival: ~ 5-10%.
  • If resected + adjuvant therapy: ~ 20-28% (best case).
  • If unresectable/metastatic: Median survival ~7 months.
Poor Prognostic Factors:
  • Lymph node involvement.
  • Tumor size >2.5 cm.
  • Vascular invasion.
  • Poor differentiation.
  • High CA 19-9 levels post-surgery.
Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas
  • Pancreatic cystic neoplasms are often incidental findings on imaging.
  • Rarely symptomatic (abdominal pain, mass, or jaundice).
  • Classified as Mucinous (premalignant/malignant) & non-mucinous (benign).
  • Management depends on size, symptoms, and malignancy risk.

1. Serous Cystadenoma (SCA)
  • Benign, non-mucinous cystic tumor.
  • More common in women (~75%), usually in the 6th-7th decade.
  • "Honeycomb" appearance on imaging (multiple small cysts).
  • Central calcification (pathognomonic but seen in <30%).
  • Slow-growing, rarely symptomatic.
Diagnosis:
  • CT/MRI: Multilocular cysts with central calcification.
  • EUS + FNA (if unclear): Low CEA & amylase, glycogen-rich cuboidal epithelium.
Management:
  • Observation unless symptomatic or large (>4 cm).
  • Resection for symptomatic cases (pain, mass effect).
2. Mucinous Cystic Neoplasm (MCN)
  • Premalignant mucinous cystic lesion (~30% risk of carcinoma).
  • Occurs exclusively in women (mean age: ~50 years).
  • Does NOT communicate with pancreatic ducts.
  • Most common in pancreatic body/tail.
  • Septated cysts with thick walls on imaging.
Diagnosis:
  • CT/MRI: Unilocular or multilocular cyst with septations, no duct communication.
  • EUS + FNA: ↑ CEA (>192 ng/mL), ↑ mucin, variable cytology.
Management:
  • Surgical resection if >3 cm, symptomatic, or has concerning features (thick walls, nodules).
  • Observation for small, asymptomatic MCNs (<3 cm).
3. Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplasm (IPMN)
  • Premalignant mucinous tumor arising from pancreatic ducts.
  • More common in men (~60%), typically age >60 years.
  • Can progress to invasive carcinoma.
  • Classified into:
  • Main Duct IPMN (high-risk, always resect).
  • Branch Duct IPMN (lower risk, selective resection).
  • Mixed Type (main + branch duct, high-risk).
Diagnosis (Sendai Guidelines)
  • Feature Worrisome Features (EUS High-Risk Stigmata (Surgery Needed) Required)
Size>3 cm>4 cm
Duct DilationMain duct 5-9 mmMain duct ≥10 mm
MuralPresent (requires EUS)Enhancing solid component

SymptomsNew-onset diabetes, pancreatitisJaundice
Management:
  • Main Duct or Mixed IPMN → Surgical resection (high malignancy risk).
  • Branch Duct IPMN (Low-risk) → Observation with imaging (MRI/EUS every 6-12 months).
4. Cystic Neuroendocrine Tumors (NETs)
  • Rare cystic variant of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.
  • Can be functional (hormone-secreting) or non-functional.
  • Seen in MEN-1 syndrome (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1).
  • Malignant potential (require resection).
Diagnosis:
  • CT/MRI: Well-defined cystic lesion with enhancing septa.
  • EUS + FNA: Chromogranin A, synaptophysin, high CEA.
  • Hormonal Workup: Insulin, gastrin, glucagon, VIP (if functional).
Management:
  • Surgical resection (due to malignancy risk).
5. Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm (SPN)
  • Rare, low-grade malignant tumor, common in young women (~30-40s).
  • Well-defined cystic mass with solid areas.
  • Slow-growing but may metastasize (low-risk).
Diagnosis:
  • CT/MRI: Large, well-circumscribed mass with solid & cystic areas.
  • EUS + FNA: β-catenin mutations, positive for synaptophysin & vimentin.
Management:
  • Surgical resection (curative in >80% of cases).

Adenoma & Adenocarcinoma of the Ampulla of Vater
  • Ampullary tumors account for ~10% of neoplasms causing distal bile duct obstruction.
  • Adenomas are benign but can progress to adenocarcinoma (premalignant).
  • Adenocarcinoma of the ampulla has a better prognosis than pancreatic cancer due to early presentation.
Clinical Presentation
  • Painless jaundice (due to biliary obstruction).
  • Intermittent jaundice & pruritus (from partial obstruction).
  • Weight loss & abdominal pain (if advanced).
  • Occult GI bleeding → Anemia, melena, or hematochezia.
  • Courvoisier’s sign (palpable gallbladder in a jaundiced patient, suggestive of malignancy).
Diagnosis
Imaging
CT scan:
  • Dilated common bile duct & pancreatic duct (Double Duct Sign).
  • Can detect metastases & local invasion.
Ultrasound (US):
  • Can show biliary duct dilation but is limited in detecting ampullary tumors.
Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP):
  • Best for direct visualization of ampullary lesions.
  • 75% of cases → Visible mass on duodenoscopy (exophytic, ulcerated, or infiltrating).
  • Biopsy via ERCP confirms diagnosis.
Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS):
  • Evaluate tumor depth & lymph node involvement.
  • Guided biopsy if ERCP biopsy is inconclusive.
Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP):
  • Non-invasive alternative to ERCP (but lacks biopsy capability).
Management
1️- Ampullary Adenoma (Benign, Premalignant)
  • If resectable → Endoscopic or Surgical Removal
  • Endoscopic Resection (for small, non-invasive tumors)
  • Surgical Resection (if not completely removable by endoscopy)
  • Surveillance after resection due to recurrence risk
2️- Ampullary Adenocarcinoma (Malignant)
  • Surgical resection is the only curative treatment
  • Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple Procedure) → Standard treatment for resectable cases.
  • Local Resection → Considered in select early-stage cases without lymph node involvement.
  • Adjuvant Chemotherapy → For advanced tumors or nodal involvement.
  • Unresectable Disease?
  • Palliative ERCP with biliary stenting → To relieve jaundice & symptoms.
  • Palliative Chemotherapy → For metastatic disease.
  • Prognosis: <1 year survival in unresectable cases.
Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors (PNETs)
  • Rare tumors (~1–5 cases per million per year).
  • Arise from islet cells of the pancreas (hormone-producing).
  • Classified as:
  • Functioning PNETs → Secrete hormones, causing distinct syndromes.
  • Non-functioning PNETs → Often found incidentally on imaging.
  • Malignancy potential varies (some benign, others aggressive with metastases).
1️- Non-Functioning PNETs
  • Most common subtype (~50-75%).
  • Usually asymptomatic, detected incidentally.
  • If symptomatic → Due to tumor mass effect:
  • Abdominal pain (most common).
  • Weight loss, jaundice, back pain (advanced cases).
  • Diagnosis:
  • CT/MRI: Enhancing pancreatic mass.
  • EUS + Biopsy → Confirm histology & malignancy potential.
  • Chromogranin A, neuron-specific enolase (NSE) → Tumor markers
  • Management:
  • <1 cm → Surveillance.
  • >2 cm or rapid growth → Surgical resection (Whipple for head lesions, distal pancreatectomy for body/tail lesions).
  • Metastatic disease → Consider debulking, chemotherapy, or targeted therapy.
2️- Functioning PNETs (Hormone-Secreting Tumors)
2A. Insulinoma (Most Common Functioning PNET)
  • Secretes Insulin → Severe fasting hypoglycemia.
  • Symptoms (Whipple’s Triad):
  • (1) Fasting or exertional hypoglycemia (<50 mg/dL).
  • (2) Symptoms of neuroglycopenia (confusion, vision changes, syncope).
  • (3) Symptom relief after glucose administration.
  • Diagnosis:
  • 72-hour fasting test → Persistent hypoglycemia with high insulin & C-peptide.
  • Imaging: CT, MRI, EUS (best for small tumors), selective arterial calcium stimulation test.
  • Management:
  • Surgical resection (enucleation if small, distal pancreatectomy or Whipple for larger tumors).
  • Diazoxide (insulin secretion blocker) or octreotide if inoperable.
2B. Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome - ZES)
  • Secretes Gastrin → Hyperacidity & refractory ulcers.
  • Symptoms:
  • Severe peptic ulcers (multiple, recurrent, or resistant to PPIs).
  • Diarrhea & steatorrhea (malabsorption from acid inactivation of pancreatic enzymes).
  • Diagnosis:
  • Serum gastrin >1000 pg/mL (definitive).
  • Secretin stimulation test (gastrin rises paradoxically).
  • CT/EUS/Somatostatin Receptor Scintigraphy (SRS) for localization.
  • Management:
  • High-dose PPIs (to control acidity).
  • Surgical resection if localized.
  • Metastatic disease → Consider somatostatin analogs, targeted therapy (sunitinib, everolimus).
2C. VIPoma (Pancreatic Cholera - WDHA Syndrome)
  • Secretes Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP) → Severe watery diarrhea (>3L/day), dehydration, & hypokalemia.
  • Symptoms:
  • Watery diarrhea (profuse, secretory, persists with fasting).
  • Hypokalemia & metabolic acidosis (HCO3 loss in stool).
  • Achlorhydria (low stomach acid production).
  • Diagnosis:
  • Serum VIP >75 pg/mL.
  • CT/MRI/EUS for tumor localization.
  • Management:
  • Somatostatin analogs (octreotide) (reduces diarrhea).
  • Surgical resection if localized.
2D. Glucagonoma (Necrolytic Migratory Erythema - NME)
  • Secretes Glucagon → Hyperglycemia & characteristic skin rash.
  • Symptoms:
  • Necrolytic Migratory Erythema (NME) → Painful, erythematous rash (legs, groin, face).
  • Diabetes Mellitus (mild to moderate).
  • Weight loss, anemia, stomatitis.
  • Diagnosis:
  • Serum glucagon >500 pg/mL.
  • CT/EUS for tumor localization.
  • Management:
  • Surgical resection if localized.
  • Somatostatin analogs (octreotide) for symptom control.
2E. Somatostatinoma
  • Secretes Somatostatin → Inhibits multiple hormones & digestive functions.
  • Symptoms:
  • Diabetes (↓ insulin).
  • Steatorrhea & malabsorption (↓ pancreatic enzymes & bile).
  • Achlorhydria (↓ acid secretion).
  • Diagnosis:
  • Serum somatostatin >30 pg/mL.
  • CT/EUS for tumor localization.
  • Management:
  • Surgical resection if localized.
  • Somatostatin analogs for symptom relief.
